query: For high-entropy alloys intended for harsh corrosive mechanical environments, what single mechanistic hypothesis could explain what governs resistance to simultaneous wear and corrosion, and why? Propose a controlled comparison that would test the hypothesis, predict how combined degradation and its wear and corrosion components would differ from a matched baseline, define where the prediction should hold or fail, identify supporting prior evidence, and state an observation that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: High-entropy alloys resist simultaneous wear and corrosion because their intrinsically homogeneous microstructure enables the rapid, dynamic formation and self-healing of a protective passivation oxide film even under mechanical disruption.
generation.material_initial_state: An as‐fabricated high‐entropy alloy with a homogeneous single-phase or near single-phase microstructure that promotes stable oxide/passivation film formation.
generation.intervention: Implement a wear–corrosion cycling test where mechanical wear cycles (e.g., sliding or impact loads) are applied in a corrosive environment (e.g., high chloride aqueous solution) to cyclically disrupt and then enable reformation of the oxide film.
generation.conditions: Testing under combined mechanical and chemical attack (e.g., cyclic sliding wear in a 3.5 wt.% NaCl solution), with comparison tests under isolated wear and isolated corrosion; the temperature and pH maintained to favor passivation film formation.
generation.structural_mediator: The dynamic passivation oxide film that continuously regenerates on the alloy surface, supported by the high configurational entropy and microstructural homogeneity of the alloy.
generation.mechanism: Mechanical wear intermittently ruptures the passive film, but the alloy’s composition and homogeneous microstructure promote rapid reformation of a protective oxide. This dynamic healing minimizes exposure of the underlying substrate, thereby synergistically reducing the extent of both wear and corrosion compared to when these degradations act independently.
generation.predicted_outcome: Under combined wear–corrosion cycling, the alloy will exhibit degradation (e.g., material loss, friction coefficient increase, pitting) that is lower than the additive effect of individual wear and corrosion tests. In contrast, alloys that lack the ability to rapidly reform the passivating film (e.g., due to minor compositional adjustments or intentional inhibitors) will show accelerated degradation.
generation.baseline: High-entropy alloy specimens tested separately under only wear conditions or only corrosion conditions, where protective film regeneration is not challenged by mechanical film rupture.
generation.boundary: This protective mechanism is expected to hold in alloys containing alloying elements that support stable oxide formation and microstructural uniformity. The hypothesis may fail in compositions lacking these features or under extreme mechanical loads that completely inhibit the film reformation process.
generation.uncertainty: The precise kinetics of film rupture and reformation under varying mechanical stresses and corrosive aggressiveness are uncertain and may depend on minor compositional nuances; the threshold at which mechanical energy overwhelms the self-healing ability is also not precisely known.

falsification_experiment.design: Conduct a controlled cycling experiment comparing two sets of high-entropy alloy specimens: one set in which the dynamic passivation process is allowed to occur naturally and a second set in which an oxide film inhibitor (or an environmental condition that suppresses oxide formation) is applied. Both sets undergo identical wear–corrosion cycling (e.g., sliding wear in a corrosive 3.5 wt.% NaCl solution) while monitoring surface film formation using in situ electrochemical impedance spectroscopy and periodic surface imaging (e.g., SEM/EDS).
measurements: Surface morphology and film continuity via SEM/EDS
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the alloy with inhibited oxide formation does not display significantly accelerated degradation (i.e., similar wear and corrosion resistance compared to the untreated specimens), this would falsify the hypothesis that dynamic passivation film reformation is the key mechanism governing resistance to simultaneous wear and corrosion.

cited_evidence.text: The addition of Zr to multielement alloys allows the improvement of some mechanical properties []; thus, in TiMoNbZrx alloy, Zr determined the improvement of wear resistance, due to the formation of an oxide film that acts as a lubricant []. In terms of corrosion resistance, grain refinement plays a great role, and a small addition of Zr can contribute to grain refinement []. Thus, our study focuses on the use of the Mo and Zr in an HEA for the manufacture of mechanical parts used in the geothermal industry at high temperature and in corrosive media. The impact of Zr addition on the CoCrFeNiMo high-entropy alloy’s microstructure, elastic modulus, and corrosion characteristics is examined in this work. In order to analyze the microstructure of the samples with and without Zr, optical microscopy, scanning electron microscopy (SEM), and energy-dispersive X-ray spectroscopy (EDS) are employed, microhardness tests are performed, a three-point bending test is used to evaluate the modulus of elasticity and linear polarization (LP), and electrochemical impedance spectroscopy (EIS) is applied to examine electrochemical responses, corrosion kinetics, and interface parameters.

In the initial stage of friction measurement, the wear mechanism of AlxCr1−xCoFeNi is adhesive wear. However, as the test time progresses, an oxide layer begins to form on the alloy’s surface, leading to a gradual increase in the friction coefficient. At this stage, the wear mechanism becomes a combination of both adhesive and abrasive wear. Once the oxidation process and the wear process have reached a dynamic equilibrium, the friction coefficient stabilizes, and the wear mechanism transitions to a state of abrasive wear. The Al0.1Cr0.9CoFeNi alloy demonstrates the lowest friction coefficient and wear rate, exhibiting values of 0.513 and 0.020 × 10−3 mm3/Nm, respectively, while the Al0.5Cr0.5CoFeNi alloy demonstrates the highest performance, with a self-corrosion voltage of 0.202 V in a 3.5 wt.% NaCl solution. Degradation of materials under various operating conditions, especially in corrosive flow environments, can seriously affect the durability of the components []. During use, components are required to withstand various forms of degradation, such as cavitation, abrasive wear, and corrosion. In turn, flow machine components such as pipelines, valves, rotors, and turbines are severely exposed to various forms of deterioration, such as slurry erosion, cavitation, and degradation under corrosive conditions, which intensify their deterioration process []. The problems associated with various wear processes require high corrosion resistance from the materials in addition to favorable mechanical properties. Among engineers, stainless steels have so far been the first choice for applications in aggressive corrosive environments []. The recent interest in HEAs (high-entropy alloys) may provide an alternative for use in corrosion-resistant steels []. To address the synergistic degradation mechanisms in engineering service environments, we propose a boron microalloying strategy to enhance the multifunctional surface performance of AlCoCrFeNiMo-based high-entropy alloys. AlCoCrFeNiMoTiBx coatings (x = 0, 0.5, 1, and 1.5) were fabricated on Q235 steel substrates using laser cladding. The microstructure of the coatings was characterized using scanning electron microscope (SEM) and energy dispersive spectrometer (EDS), while their wear and corrosion resistance were evaluated through tribological and electrochemical tests. The key findings indicate that boron addition preserves the original body-centered cubic (BCC) and σ phases in the coating while promoting the in situ formation of TiB2, leading to lattice distortion. With increasing B content, the BCC phase becomes refined, and both the fraction and size of TiB2 particles increase. Boron incorporation improves the coating’s microhardness and wear resistance, with the highest wear resistance achieved at x = 1, where abrasive and oxidative wear predominate. frame.system: High‐entropy alloys in their as‐fabricated microstructural state, intended for use in harsh, corrosive mechanical environments where both wear and corrosion processes are active.
frame.goal: To identify and validate a single mechanistic hypothesis that unifies the understanding of resistance to simultaneous wear and corrosion in these alloys.
frame.limitation: A lack of an integrated mechanism that explains why and how the microstructural features and composition of high‐entropy alloys confer a combined resistance to wear and corrosion under aggressive environmental and mechanical conditions.
constraints: The hypothesis must be testable via a controlled comparison with a matched baseline, isolating the contributions of wear and corrosion.
Evaluation should predict differences in degradation when wear and corrosion act concurrently versus individually.
The prediction should include conditions where the hypothesis is expected to hold and conditions under which it might fail.
A falsifying observation must be defined clearly.
frame.regime: Environments combining significant mechanical wear (e.g., sliding or impact stresses) and aggressive corrosion (e.g., high chloride or acidic conditions), where the synergistic interaction between mechanical damage and chemical attack is prominent.
prior_attempts: Previous studies have often separated wear and corrosion testing, addressing each degradation mode individually rather than in concert.
Empirical observations have been made in high-entropy alloys without a unifying model, often failing to predict the performance under combined degradation.
Attempts to link specific microstructural phases to wear or corrosion resistance separately have fallen short of explaining their simultaneous interaction.
frame.understanding: A promising mechanistic hypothesis is that the alloy’s ability to form and maintain a dynamic, self-healing passivation film during mechanical disruption governs its combined degradation resistance. This film, promoted by the high configurational entropy and the resulting microstructural stability, adapts under wear conditions by continually reforming, thereby mitigating the exposure of the substrate to corrosive species. The synergy between rapid film regeneration and microstructural homogeneity is proposed as the key factor, explaining why the alloy performs better under simultaneous wear and corrosion compared to the sum of its individual contributions.
